newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr dithers, needs rate decision.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr dithers, needs rate decision.

text.p: The Australian dollar dithered to yet another directionless finish Thursday as soft housing data came and went without disturbing the market's rate vigil.

What action there was came on the crosses, where traders reported good two-way flows against the yen including more samurai-related demand, spillover profit-taking from a retreating US$/yen and straight sales from Japanese corporates.

An unexpected dive in building approvals offered further reason to expect a cut in domestic interest rates next week, but this has been so long discounted that only the real thing would spring the currency from its long US$0.7850/7985 confinement.
By 4.45 pm (0445 GMT) the local dollar was putting down roots at US$0.7917/22 from an early US$0.7916/21 and US$0.7911/16 late here Wednesday.

It did lose ground on the yen to 90.08/18 yen from 90.20/30 late yesterday, but managed to keep a grip on the psychological 90.00 level despite repeated attempts by speculators to trigger stop loss sales below there.

The lapse was partly attributed to a pullback in US$/yen to 113.75/80 yen from 114.10/15, but dealers also reported straight AUD/yen selling with one Japanese corporate thought to have dumped as much as A$200 million.
In trade weighted terms it eased to 58.6 from 58.7.

There were signs of more samurai linked buying, with traders expecting the recent rush of new yen/A$ issues -- four bonds so far this week worth a total 110 billion yen -- to continue while Japanese bond rates keep falling.
The 10-year JGB yield reached a fresh 15-month low of 2.515 percent today, while the Australian 10-year bond was paying a relatively rich 7.41 percent.
Traders remained concerned that offshore investors could take fright if, as most in the market expect, the Reserve Bank cut official rates after its board meeting next week.
Market odds on an easing shortened a little further today following a soft set of domestic building data.
September building approvals slid 8.6 percent when analysts had looked for a flat outcome or at worse a 3.0 percent fall.

The drop almost wiped out the 1.6 and 8.1 percent gains seen in August and July respectively and swung the trend measure for the three months to slightly negative when it had originally been showing modest growth.
There was a saving grace in the figures in that approvals for private homes, which make up over 70 percent of the dwelling building market, rose a robust 2.8 percent.
All the weakness was in the medium to high density residential sector which was notoriously volatile and apt to bounce back in October, analysts said.

"The data confirm the subdued conditions facing the residential constuction sector, but is not suggestive of any renewed downward trend in housing activity," said Michael Blythe, a senior economist at Commonwealth Bank.

"Neither it it likely to have added anything new to monetary policy deliberations," he said. "Our inflation performance, current and prospective, remains consistent with a near term cut in official rates."
Domestic data on September retail sales, due Friday, are also expected to show some slowing on the demand side, although sales for the quarter ought to be healthy enough.

Median forecast are for a 0.5 percent dip after gains of 1.1 and 1.0 percent in August and July respectively. Real sales for the quarter, adjusted for inflation, were seen rising 1.3 percent in a big turnaround from the 0.6 percent fall in the June quarter.
Such a jump would add around 0.3 point to the expenditure based measure of gross domestic product (GDP-E) for the quarter.
